items.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: Coltrane, played with — Earl Bostic Rhythm & Blues band.

ctx.x: Did you guys kind of have a separate half from the rock & roll and the pop music that was played on AM radio at the time? In other words, did you listen to the music that was getting all the airplay, the Chuck Berry and those guys? Did it affect you at all? © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

If it was good music yeah. And to this day I still do that because see I always tell people — somebody asked me a question and I said well you know I consider myself a blues piano player that understands the philosophy of jazz. So I told Fred and he said, “You said that?” He said, “I like that.” That’s what I am. I’m going to always be, because blues or jazz comes from the blues. Because here again, like I said, not to be redundant, there are a lot of jazz musicians who can swing, who can play jazz, but they…

and he was from Greenwood, Mississippi where Mulgrew Miller is from. Little Milton Campbell. He could sing “If Walls Could Talk” and “Poor Man Blues” you see. And see in Chicago you had to play the blues, not in New York City. You go on the south side of Chicago or the west side, and you had to know how to play some blues. And you had to know how to play for singers. And see those are the two foundations. So when I got to Chicago it was no big deal ‘cause I already knew kind of how to play the blues from being in…
